parts.title: The night train
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, I travelled from Paris to Vienna on a night train. I had always travelled by plane before, but my brother said that trains were more relaxing, so I decided to try one. The train left at seven in the evening, and I shared a small cabin with three strangers.

At first, I felt awkward, but one of the passengers, a retired teacher called Maria, offered me some biscuits and began to tell stories about her trips. Soon we were all laughing. When the lights went out, I climbed into the narrow bed at the top. The movement of the train was gentle, and, surprisingly, I fell asleep quickly.

I woke up at six, just as we were crossing the mountains. The sun was rising, and the snow looked pink. I stood in the corridor with a cup of coffee, watching the view for an hour. That was the most beautiful moment of my holiday.

Of course, the trip took much longer than a flight would have done, and the shower was tiny. But I arrived feeling rested, and I had made three new friends. Next year, I plan to try the night train to Rome.

questions.explanation: Her brother said that trains were more relaxing.

She climbed into the bed at the top and fell asleep quickly.

questions.explanation: She watched the view of the mountains and the pink snow for an hour.

options: Fly all the way to Rome
questions.explanation: She plans to try the night train to Rome.

parts.title: The first railways
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
The first railways did not use steam engines at all. [1] Horses pulled wagons along wooden or iron tracks, because this was easier than pulling them over muddy roads.

In 1804, an engineer built the first steam locomotive to run on rails. [2] It could carry ten tons of iron and seventy men, but it was so heavy that it broke the track.

About twenty years later, the first public railway opened in England. [3] Passengers could now travel between two towns much faster than by horse.

Railways changed people's lives quickly. [4] Fresh fish and milk could reach cities within hours, and workers could live far from their factories.

By 1900, there were railways on every continent except one. [5] Today, high-speed trains travel at three hundred kilometres an hour, and many countries are building new lines.
sentences: At that time, only the rich could afford to ride in them.
Some stations are famous for their beautiful clocks.
It was impressive, but it was not yet practical.
A steam engine pulled the carriages, and the public could buy tickets.
Instead, the power came from animals.
Food and goods could now travel much farther than before.
Horses were still used to pull wagons in cities until the 1920s.
Since then, trains have become faster and more comfortable.

gaps.explanation: The power came from animals, as the next sentence says horses pulled the wagons.
The first locomotive was impressive but not practical, because it broke the track.
A steam engine pulled the carriages and tickets were sold; the next sentence says passengers could travel faster.
Goods could travel farther; the next sentence gives fresh fish and milk as examples.
Since then trains have become faster; the next sentence describes high-speed trains today.

parts.title: A message about a late train
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Chet, I am writing to tell you about my journey to your city. The train left [1] time, and I found a seat next to the window. About halfway there, the train [2] suddenly because of a problem on the line. We waited for almost an hour, and many passengers started to complain [3] the delay. Fortunately, a station worker came to explain the situation, and a few minutes later we were moving again. I arrived [4] than I had planned, so I missed my first meeting. Next time, I will leave earlier. I will tell you the time of my [5] as soon as I know it. I will be at platform four, [6] you can find me easily. Garan

questions.explanation: On time means at the planned time.
A train stops because of a problem on the line.
We complain about something.
After than we need a comparative: later than I had planned.
After my we need a noun: the time of my arrival.
So gives the result: I will be at platform four, so you can find me.

parts.title: Why people love trains
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: More and more people are choosing to travel [1] train instead of by plane. One reason is that stations are usually in the centre of cities, [2] airports are often far away. Another advantage is comfort. On a train, you can stand up, walk around and even have a meal. [3] a plane, you must stay in your seat for hours. A journey by train produces much less carbon than the same journey by air. Of course, trains are not perfect. Tickets can be expensive if you [4] not book early, and delays do happen. [5] spite of this, many travellers say that they would never go back to flying. They say that the extra time is [6] small price to pay.

gaps.explanation: By train is the fixed phrase for the means of transport.
The sentence contrasts stations in the centre with airports far away.
On a plane contrasts with on a train.
The negative present simple needs do not.
In spite of this is a fixed phrase.
A small price to pay is a fixed phrase.

parts.title: A welcome at the heritage railway
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: manager
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Heritage Railway. My name is Chet, and I am the station manager. Our steam train runs from this station to the lake and back. The whole journey takes fifty minutes. It used to be forty minutes, but we now go slowly so that you can enjoy the view. Trains leave every hour, starting at ten, and the last one leaves at four o’clock. In August we add a train at half past, but today we have only the normal timetable. Let me tell you about prices. A return ticket for an adult costs twelve pounds. For children it’s six, and a family ticket is thirty. The price includes a hot drink. If you want a single ticket, it is eight pounds, but most people prefer a return. Now, a tip for photographs. Most visitors go to the first carriage, because it’s near the engine, but it’s very noisy and full of smoke. The last carriage is the best place, because you can look back along the line. The big windows open, so be careful. Along the way, we cross an old stone bridge. It has stood here for more than a hundred years, and it was built by hand. The tunnel after that is even older. At the lake, the train stops for forty minutes. You can have a snack at the café, or walk around the water. Boat trips only run in the summer, but there’s a playground for children, with a slide and a wooden train. Please keep an eye on little ones. We leave exactly at the time on your ticket, and the whistle will blow two minutes before. Enjoy the ride!

gaps.prompt: A trip to the lake and back takes ___ minutes
gaps.explanation: The whole journey takes fifty minutes; forty minutes was the old time.

gaps.prompt: Trains depart from the station every ___
gaps.explanation: Trains leave every hour; the extra August train comes at half past.

gaps.prompt: An adult's return ticket costs ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: A return costs twelve pounds; six is the child price and eight is a single.

gaps.prompt: For the best photographs, sit in the last ___
gaps.explanation: The first carriage is noisy and smoky; the last carriage is the best place.

gaps.prompt: The stone bridge has stood for more than a hundred ___
gaps.explanation: The bridge is more than a hundred years old and the tunnel is even older.

gaps.prompt: At the lake, children can use the ___
gaps.explanation: Boat trips only run in summer; the children have a playground.

parts.title: An interview with a train driver
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Garan, why did you choose to be a train driver?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People assume my father drove trains, but he was a baker. And I like travelling, but you could do that as a passenger. The real reason is simple: I loved watching trains. As a boy I sat on a bridge with a notebook and wrote down every number. I never grew out of it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: When does your working day begin?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It depends on the shift. Sometimes I start at seven in the evening and work all night, and I have done midnight starts too. But this week I begin at five in the morning, which means getting up at four. It’s dark and cold, but I like the quiet.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is the job stressful?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not on Sundays, there are fewer trains. Heat isn’t a problem, the cabin has air conditioning. Bad weather is what worries me: fog, ice and heavy rain make the rails slippery, and I need to be careful with every bend. That’s when I feel under pressure.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you like best about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s not the people, although passengers wave to me at stations, and it’s not the breaks, which are short. For me it’s summer mornings. When the sun rises over the fields and there’s mist on the river, I think this is the best office in the world.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Has anything surprising happened to you?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Once. The train was on time and the signals were fine, but a family of ducks was walking across the line, just in front of me. I stopped and waited five minutes until they were safe. The passengers thought we had a technical problem.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What would you say about the job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: You must be happy on your own, because you spend hours without talking to anyone. It’s not easy to learn quickly, because the training takes two years, and the pay is just OK. But if you like your own company, it’s wonderful.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do passengers ever ask you for help?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: At the station, yes, all the time. People ask me which platform to use, or what time the next train leaves. I always smile, and I tell them to look at the board, then I help them anyway.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Thank you, Garan. One last question: would you do it again?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: In a second. I still feel excited every time I leave a station. The boy with the notebook is still inside me.
